punjab.name: Punjab
punjab.tagline: Fertile plains, winter fields and a food culture shaped by farming and hospitality.
punjab.geography: Punjab lies in the north-western Indus plains. The Sutlej, Beas and Ravi, fertile soils and canal irrigation support wheat, mustard, pulses and dairy. Cool winters bring leafy greens to the table; migration and trade have also shaped regional food.
punjab.culinaryLandscape: Punjabi food varies by district and community. Wheat breads, dairy, pulses, mustard greens and tandoor cooking are widely recognised, alongside langar traditions and a strong street-food culture.

dishes.name: Sarson da Saag with Makki di Roti
dishes.descriptor: Winter greens with maize flatbread
dishes.overview: A winter meal of slow-cooked mustard greens with hand-patted maize flatbread. It is often finished with ghee or white butter and served with radish, jaggery or lassi.
steps: Wash and chop the greens. Simmer with ginger, garlic, chillies, salt and a little water until soft.
Mash or blend coarsely. Add a little maize-flour slurry if a thicker saag is preferred.
Temper with ghee, garlic and optional onion; simmer until combined.
Mix maize flour with warm water and salt. Pat into flat rounds by hand.
Cook on a hot griddle, turning carefully. Finish with ghee or butter and serve with the saag.
dishes.history: The pairing grew from seasonal farming and household cooking; no single inventor is documented. Mustard greens are a winter crop. Maize reached India after the Columbian exchange, but its route and timing remain debated. Makki di roti is best understood as part of an evolving Punjabi food tradition, not an unchanged ancient staple.

dishes.name: Chole Bhature
dishes.descriptor: Spiced chickpeas with puffed fried bread
dishes.overview: Spiced chickpeas simmered in a thick masala and served with deep-fried, leavened bhature. Pickled onion, chutney and green chilli often accompany it.
ingredients: Coriander, cumin, chilli and garam masala
Maida or wheat flour, yoghurt and leavening
steps: Soak chickpeas overnight and cook until tender.
Cook onion, ginger and garlic. Add tomato and spices to make a thick masala.
Add chickpeas and some cooking liquid; simmer until the gravy thickens.
Make a soft dough with flour, yoghurt, salt and leavening. Rest, then roll into rounds.
Deep-fry until puffed and golden. Serve hot with the chole.
dishes.history: Chickpea curries and fried breads have longer, separate histories across North India; the pairing's exact origin is disputed. A family account from Sita Ram Diwan Chand describes selling chole bhature from a pushcart in Paharganj after Partition. It documents one influential Delhi story, not the dish's sole invention.

west-bengal.name: West Bengal
west-bengal.tagline: A river-and-delta cuisine shaped by rice, fish, mustard and sweets.
west-bengal.geography: West Bengal runs from the Himalayan foothills to the Ganga delta and Bay of Bengal. Rivers, ponds and wetlands support freshwater fish; rice, mustard, vegetables and coastal produce shape everyday cooking.
west-bengal.culinaryLandscape: Bengali food often pairs rice with fish, vegetables and mustard-based preparations. Milk sweets are also important. Recipes differ between the hills, delta, coast and city kitchens.

dishes.name: Shorshe Ilish
dishes.descriptor: Hilsa cooked with mustard and green chilli
dishes.overview: Hilsa is cooked in a pungent mustard paste with green chillies, turmeric and mustard oil. It may be steamed or gently simmered; the sharp sauce balances the fish's rich flavour.
steps: Soak mustard seeds briefly, then grind with green chillies, salt and a little water.
Rub the fish with turmeric and salt.
Warm mustard oil. Add the mustard paste with water and green chillies.
Add the fish and steam or simmer gently until just cooked. Avoid stirring roughly.
dishes.history: Hilsa has long been part of Bengal's river and estuary foodways. Mustard oil is now a defining flavour, but its social status changed over time. Food historian Chitrita Banerji notes that some nineteenth-century elite households in Calcutta did not readily accept it. This shows how regional tastes also evolve.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated hilsa landings, Hooghly fish markets, river fishing or Bengali household kitchens. Record the collection and date.

dishes.name: Banglar Rosogolla
dishes.descriptor: Chhana dumplings poached in sugar syrup
dishes.overview: Fresh chhana is kneaded into smooth balls, cooked in boiling sugar syrup and left to soak. The texture depends on the chhana, kneading and syrup.
ingredients: A little semolina or flour in some versions
steps: Curdle hot milk with lemon juice or another food acid; drain the chhana in a clean cloth.
Rinse and press until moist but not watery.
Knead until smooth and roll into crack-free balls.
Boil sugar and water. Add the balls with enough room to expand.
Cook until spongy, then cool in the syrup before serving.
dishes.history: The history of rasgulla is contested between Odisha and Bengal, and the surviving record is incomplete. Bengal's modern commercial story is strongly linked with Nabin Chandra Das in nineteenth-century Calcutta. This entry documents the Bengali tradition without claiming an uncontested single origin.

tamil-nadu.name: Tamil Nadu
tamil-nadu.tagline: A varied food culture shaped by paddy fields, dry plains, coastal trade and temple towns.
tamil-nadu.geography: Tamil Nadu includes the Coromandel coast, Kaveri delta, dry interior plains and southern uplands. Rice is central in many areas; millets, pulses, coconut, tamarind and spices vary by region.
tamil-nadu.culinaryLandscape: Tamil Nadu has distinct food traditions in Chettinad, Kongunadu, the Kaveri delta, Madurai and the coast. Rice dishes, lentils, fermented foods and festival preparations are common, but recipes vary locally.

dishes.name: Sakkarai Pongal
dishes.descriptor: Sweet rice and lentils for the harvest festival
dishes.overview: Rice and moong dal are cooked until soft, then sweetened with jaggery and finished with ghee, cardamom, cashews and raisins. It is closely associated with Thai Pongal.
steps: Rinse the rice and roast the moong dal lightly.
Cook both with water or milk until very soft.
Dissolve jaggery in a little water and strain.
Stir the syrup into the rice mixture and simmer briefly.
Finish with ghee, cardamom, cashews and raisins.
dishes.history: Thai Pongal is a January harvest festival. Families cook rice as an offering of thanks for the harvest, the Sun and cattle. Sweet pongal is a festive preparation, but the exact origin date of today's recipe is not established by the sources used here.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated Pongal celebrations, outdoor cooking pots, paddy harvests or family festival photographs. Preserve the original caption and date.

dishes.name: Chicken Chettinad
dishes.descriptor: Chicken in a freshly ground, aromatic spice masala
dishes.overview: Chicken is simmered in a freshly ground masala that often includes pepper, fennel, dried chillies, coconut and local spices. Recipes differ between Chettinad households.
ingredients: Dried red chillies, cinnamon and cloves
Kalpasi or other local spices, where used
steps: Dry-roast the whole spices and coconut; cool and grind.
Sauté curry leaves, onion, ginger and garlic in oil.
Add tomato and the ground masala. Cook until aromatic.
Add chicken, salt and a little water. Cover and cook until tender.
Reduce the gravy to the preferred consistency and finish with curry leaves.
dishes.history: Chettinad is associated with the Nattukottai Chettiar community of Tamil Nadu. Its trading networks and travel helped shape a cuisine known for layered spice blends. Chicken Chettinad is a regional style, not one fixed recipe with a known inventor.

kerala.name: Kerala
kerala.tagline: A coastal and backwater cuisine built around rice, coconut, spices and shared meals.
kerala.geography: Kerala lies between the Arabian Sea and Western Ghats. Monsoon rainfall, backwaters, paddy fields and spice-growing hills support rice, coconut, plantain, pepper, ginger and a wide range of fish and vegetables.
kerala.culinaryLandscape: Kerala food includes banana-leaf feasts, rice breakfasts, coconut-rich curries and coastal fish dishes. Malabar, central Kerala and Travancore have distinct traditions.

dishes.name: Kerala Sadya
dishes.descriptor: A ceremonial vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf
dishes.overview: Sadya is a ceremonial vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf. Rice is accompanied by curries, vegetable dishes, pickles, savouries and payasam; the exact menu varies.
ingredients: Curry leaves, mustard seeds and chillies
steps: Prepare the dishes separately: dal, sambar, avial, thoran, olan, pachadi and pickles are common examples.
Cook the rice and place a clean banana leaf before the guest.
Arrange the accompaniments in the customary order; local practice varies.
Serve rice with the curries and side dishes.
Finish with payasam and the customary savouries.
dishes.history: Sadya is a form of festive hospitality in Kerala, not a single recipe. Onam sadya is its best-known form, but similar feasts are served at weddings and other celebrations. Kerala Tourism documents the leaf arrangement, serving customs and regional variations.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated Onam feasts, wedding sadya service or community banana-leaf meals. Identify the event, location, date and photographer.

dishes.name: Puttu and Kadala Curry
dishes.descriptor: Steamed rice cylinders with black-chickpea curry
dishes.overview: Puttu is steamed rice flour layered with grated coconut. It is commonly served with kadala curry, a spiced black-chickpea preparation.
ingredients: Onion or shallots, ginger and garlic
Coconut oil, mustard seeds and curry leaves
steps: Soak black chickpeas overnight and cook until tender.
Roast coconut, shallots, chilli and coriander; grind to a paste.
Temper mustard seeds and curry leaves. Add onion, chickpeas and the paste; simmer.
Moisten rice flour with salted water until crumbly, not dough-like.
Layer rice flour and coconut in a puttu steamer; steam until cooked.
dishes.history: Puttu and kadala curry are a familiar breakfast pairing in Kerala. The dish uses rice flour and coconut, while the curry uses black chickpeas. Kerala Tourism documents the preparation, but does not establish a single inventor or exact origin date.
dishes.imageHint: Search dated Kerala kitchen photographs, traditional puttu steamers or household breakfast scenes. Do not label a modern utensil as antique.

rajasthan.name: Rajasthan
rajasthan.tagline: A cuisine shaped by arid landscapes, durable ingredients and hospitality.
rajasthan.geography: Rajasthan includes the Thar Desert, Aravalli range and semi-arid plains. Water scarcity and seasonal produce encouraged the use of pulses, gram flour, millet, wheat, dairy and preserved foods.
rajasthan.culinaryLandscape: Rajasthani food is more than royal cuisine. Everyday meals use breads, pulses, dairy, gram flour and preserved vegetables. Dishes differ between desert districts, eastern plains and Mewar.

dishes.name: Dal Baati Churma
dishes.descriptor: Baked wheat rolls, lentils and sweetened crushed bread
dishes.overview: Baati (firm wheat rolls) is served with lentil dal and churma, a sweet made from crushed wheat and ghee. It is a well-known Rajasthani meal served at family gatherings and feasts.
steps: Make a firm wheat dough with ghee, salt and water; shape into balls.
Bake or roast the baati until browned and cooked through.
Cook the lentils until soft; temper with ghee and spices.
Crush some baati and mix with jaggery or sugar and ghee for churma.
Serve baati with dal, churma and chutney.
dishes.history: Dal baati churma is strongly associated with Rajasthan. A popular legend links baati to Mewar ruler Bappa Rawal, but clear evidence for that specific story is limited. The better-supported context is practical: wheat, pulses and ghee suit local food economies and can be cooked with simple equipment and fuel.
dishes.imageHint: Look for archival Mewar kitchens, clay ovens, traditional baati roasting or dated feast photographs. Do not illustrate the Bappa Rawal legend as fact.

dishes.name: Gatte ki Sabzi
dishes.descriptor: Gram-flour dumplings in a spiced yoghurt gravy
dishes.overview: Seasoned gram-flour dough is shaped into logs, boiled and sliced. The pieces are simmered in a tangy yoghurt gravy.
steps: Mix besan with salt, spices, carom seeds and a little oil; add water to form a firm dough.
Roll into logs and simmer in salted water until cooked.
Cool and slice the logs into discs.
Whisk yoghurt with spices and a little water.
Temper cumin and asafoetida, add the yoghurt mixture and gatte, then simmer gently.
dishes.history: Rajasthan Foundation notes that arid conditions and limited fresh vegetables helped make gram flour, grains and dairy important in the state's food. Gatte uses stored besan to make a filling dish. The available sources do not establish a single origin story or inventor.

gujarat.name: Gujarat
gujarat.tagline: A cuisine of seasonal vegetables, grains, pulses and fermented foods.
gujarat.geography: Gujarat spans the Rann of Kutch, Kathiawar, river plains and the coast. Its dry and fertile zones support different crops, including millets, pulses, vegetables and dairy produce.
gujarat.culinaryLandscape: Gujarati food includes farsan, fermented batters, vegetable dishes, breads and seasonal one-pot meals. Vegetarian traditions are strong in many communities, while coastal foodways also include fish.

dishes.name: Undhiyu
dishes.descriptor: Winter vegetables slow-cooked in an inverted clay pot
dishes.overview: Undhiyu combines winter vegetables, beans, stuffed aubergines and methi muthia. Traditionally, the ingredients are layered in a clay pot and slow-cooked.
steps: Grind green garlic, coriander, coconut, sesame, spices and lemon into a coarse masala.
Stuff the aubergines and cut the other vegetables.
Make methi muthia with fenugreek leaves, gram flour and spices.
Layer vegetables and muthia in a heavy pot with masala and a little water.
Cover and cook slowly until tender; turn gently.
dishes.history: Undhiyu is associated with the winter harvest of south Gujarat, especially Surat. Gujarat Tourism describes cooking vegetables in a clay pot called a matla, placed upside down over heat. The name is linked to undhu, Gujarati for 'upside down'.

dishes.name: Dhokla
dishes.descriptor: A soft, savoury steamed batter preparation
dishes.overview: Dhokla is a savoury steamed cake made from fermented rice-and-pulse batter or, in popular versions, gram flour. It is cut into pieces and finished with a mustard-seed and curry-leaf tempering.
ingredients: Rice and chana dal, or gram flour depending on style
Natural fermentation or fruit salt for quick versions
steps: For a fermented version, soak rice and chana dal, grind and leave until aerated.
Season with salt, ginger and chilli. Add fruit salt only for a quick version.
Pour into a greased pan and steam until set.
Cool slightly and cut into squares.
Temper mustard seeds, curry leaves and chillies in oil; pour over the dhokla.
dishes.history: A 2022 review in the Journal of Applied Microbiology notes a reference to a possible precursor called dukkia in Gujarati Jain literature dated to 1066 CE. This is not proof that today's dhokla recipe existed unchanged then. Khaman, made mainly from gram flour, is related but distinct.

maharashtra.name: Maharashtra
maharashtra.tagline: From Deccan grain kitchens to Mumbai street stalls, food reflects regional life and migration.
maharashtra.geography: Maharashtra stretches from the Konkan coast across the Western Ghats to the Deccan plateau and Vidarbha. Coastal cooking uses rice, coconut and fish; the interior uses jowar, bajra, pulses and groundnuts.
maharashtra.culinaryLandscape: Konkan, Desh, Vidarbha, Khandesh and Mumbai have distinct food traditions. Bhakri meals, lentil dishes, festival sweets and city snacks form part of this varied cuisine.

dishes.name: Vada Pav
dishes.descriptor: Spiced potato fritter served in a soft bread roll
dishes.overview: A spiced potato fritter is coated in gram-flour batter, deep-fried and served inside a pav roll. Garlic chutney, green chutney and fried chilli are common accompaniments.
ingredients: Mustard seeds, turmeric and curry leaves
Dry garlic chutney and green chutney
steps: Boil and mash potatoes. Mix with a tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves, turmeric, chilli, ginger and garlic.
Shape the potato mixture into balls.
Make a thick gram-flour batter with salt and turmeric.
Dip the balls in batter and deep-fry until crisp.
Serve inside pav with chutneys and fried chilli.
dishes.history: Vada pav is a modern Mumbai street food. A 2015 Cultural Anthropology study traces its parts to different food histories: pav to Portuguese-influenced and migrant bakery culture, and vada to regional snack traditions. The story that vendor Ashok Vaidya paired them in the 1960s is widely reported, but not proven as the only origin.
dishes.imageHint: Search dated 1960s–1980s Mumbai street stalls, Dadar vendors, mill-worker food scenes or early vada-pav carts. Treat the Ashok Vaidya story as a reported origin.

dishes.name: Puran Poli
dishes.descriptor: Sweet lentil-and-jaggery flatbread
dishes.overview: A thin flatbread is filled with cooked chana dal and jaggery, flavoured with cardamom or nutmeg. It is griddled and usually served with ghee.
steps: Cook chana dal until tender; drain well.
Cook the dal with jaggery until thick, then mash until smooth.
Add cardamom and nutmeg; cool the filling.
Knead a soft flour dough and let it rest.
Wrap the filling in dough, roll gently and cook on a hot griddle with ghee.
dishes.history: Puran poli is a festive sweet in Maharashtra, including at Gudi Padwa. A food-technology review cites a related preparation called purana in the twelfth-century text Manasollasa. This is an antecedent reference, not proof that today's recipe was identical.

karnataka.name: Karnataka
karnataka.tagline: A varied food culture, from coastal rice dishes to the millet traditions of the Deccan.
karnataka.geography: Karnataka spans the Konkan and Malnad, the Kaveri basin, the dry Deccan plateau and northern districts. Rice, ragi, jowar, pulses, coconut and tamarind are used differently across these regions.
karnataka.culinaryLandscape: Coastal, Udupi, Kodava, North Karnataka and Mysuru-Bengaluru cuisines are distinct. Everyday millet meals, tiffin dishes, temple foodways and festival sweets all have a place.

dishes.name: Mysore Pak
dishes.descriptor: A ghee-rich sweet of gram flour and sugar
dishes.overview: Mysore Pak is made by cooking gram flour with ghee and sugar syrup until it sets. It may be soft and porous or firmer and crumbly.
steps: Sieve gram flour and roast lightly in some ghee.
Prepare a sugar syrup.
Add the flour gradually, stirring to prevent lumps.
Add hot ghee in batches and stir until the mixture thickens.
Pour into a greased tray, set and cut while slightly warm.
dishes.history: Mysore Pak is linked by local tradition to the Mysore Palace kitchen during the Wadiyar period. The popular story names palace cook Kakasura Madappa. A descendant's account preserves this family memory, but it is not a surviving palace recipe record.

dishes.name: Bisi Bele Bath
dishes.descriptor: Hot rice, lentils, vegetables and tamarind
dishes.overview: A hot rice-and-lentil dish cooked with vegetables, tamarind and a roasted spice blend. It is often finished with ghee, cashews and curry leaves.
ingredients: Carrot, beans, peas or other vegetables
Chana dal, urad dal and dry coconut for masala
steps: Cook rice and toor dal until soft; cook the vegetables until tender.
Roast and grind the spices with lentils and dry coconut.
Prepare tamarind extract and add it to the vegetables.
Combine rice, dal, vegetables, tamarind and spice powder; simmer until thick.
Finish with a ghee tempering of cashews and curry leaves.
dishes.history: Bisi bele bath is associated with the Mysuru-Bengaluru region. Its name means 'hot lentil-rice'. Tourism sources document its ingredients and popularity, but do not establish a reliable inventor or exact origin date; a palace-invention story is therefore not used here.

uttar-pradesh.name: Uttar Pradesh
uttar-pradesh.tagline: A broad food landscape shaped by the Ganga plains, pilgrimage towns and Awadh's kitchens.
uttar-pradesh.geography: Uttar Pradesh spans the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, eastern plains, Terai foothills and historic Awadh. Wheat, rice, pulses, dairy and seasonal vegetables shape everyday meals; river fish is important in some areas.
uttar-pradesh.culinaryLandscape: The state includes Awadhi slow-cooked dishes, Banarasi street food, western UP breads and dairy, and eastern UP rice and lentils. Lucknow's kebabs are one regional tradition, not the whole state's cuisine.

dishes.name: Galouti Kebab
dishes.descriptor: Fine-textured minced meat kebab from Lucknow
dishes.overview: Finely minced meat is mixed with raw papaya, aromatics and spices, shaped into small patties and shallow-fried in ghee. It is often served with paratha or roomali roti.
steps: Grind the meat until very fine.
Mix with papaya, ginger-garlic, fried onion and spices.
Rest briefly so the papaya can tenderise the meat.
Shape into small, flat patties.
Cook gently in ghee until set and lightly browned.
dishes.history: Galouti kebab belongs to Lucknow's Awadhi kebab tradition. A popular story links its soft texture to Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula's difficulty chewing, but this is a culinary legend, not a dated kitchen record. The wider context is the refinement of minced-meat kebabs in Awadh.

dishes.name: Awadhi Dum Pukht Biryani
dishes.descriptor: Rice and meat slowly cooked in a sealed vessel
dishes.overview: Marinated meat and partly cooked rice are layered in a heavy vessel, sealed with dough and cooked slowly. The trapped steam finishes the rice and meat together.
steps: Marinate the meat with yoghurt, ginger-garlic, fried onion and spices.
Parboil the rice with whole spices; drain while still firm.
Layer meat and rice in a heavy handi with herbs and ghee.
Seal the lid with dough to keep steam inside.
Cook over low heat until the meat and rice are done; rest before opening.
dishes.history: Dum pukht means slow cooking in a sealed vessel and is closely associated with Lucknow's Awadhi food culture. Popular stories about its origin are difficult to verify. This entry focuses on the documented cooking method and its regional association, not a single inventor.

assam.name: Assam
assam.tagline: A riverine cuisine of rice, freshwater fish, sour broths and banana-ash preparations.
assam.geography: Assam is shaped by the Brahmaputra and Barak valleys, wetlands, floodplains and heavy monsoon rainfall. Rice, freshwater fish, banana plants, bamboo shoots and souring fruits are important in many local foodways.
assam.culinaryLandscape: Assamese meals may include khar, an alkaline preparation, and tenga, a light sour curry, with rice, greens and fish. Ingredients and recipes vary across the state's communities.

dishes.name: Assamese Khar
dishes.descriptor: An alkaline preparation made with plant-ash filtrate
dishes.overview: Khar is both an alkaline cooking ingredient and dishes made with it. Kola khar is filtered from banana-plant ash and used in preparations with papaya, pulses or vegetables.
steps: Prepare kola khar using a documented food-safe household method for banana-plant ash.
After the ash cools, pass water through it and filter the liquid. Never use unknown or treated ash.
Cook papaya, pulses or vegetables until nearly tender.
Add a measured amount of khar filtrate and simmer briefly.
Serve with rice. Ingredients and methods vary by household.
dishes.history: Khar is an Assamese food technique, not just a seasoning. A 2020 Journal of Ethnic Foods study documents banana trunk, rhizome and peels being dried, burned and filtered with water to make kolakhar. The method reflects local plant knowledge and household practice.

dishes.name: Masor Tenga
dishes.descriptor: Light, sour fish curry with seasonal ingredients
dishes.overview: A light fish curry with a gentle sourness. Tomato, lemon, thekera, elephant apple, roselle or raw mango may be used, depending on season and household.
steps: Clean the fish and rub with turmeric and salt.
Lightly fry the pieces in mustard oil; set aside.
Temper whole spices and add tomato or another souring ingredient.
Add water and simmer to make a light broth.
Return the fish and simmer gently until cooked; finish with chilli and herbs.
dishes.history: Masor tenga is a familiar sour fish preparation in Assam. Assam Tourism lists several local souring ingredients, showing that tenga is a flexible method shaped by season and produce rather than one fixed recipe with a known inventor.

andhra-pradesh.name: Andhra Pradesh
andhra-pradesh.tagline: Coastal and river-valley food shaped by rice, chillies and tamarind.
andhra-pradesh.geography: Andhra Pradesh runs from the Deccan plateau to the Bay of Bengal. The Krishna and Godavari deltas support rice farming, while the drier Rayalaseema interior grows more millets and pulses. The coast also supplies fish; tamarind, chillies and sesame are widely used.
andhra-pradesh.culinaryLandscape: Andhra food often pairs rice with lentils, sour tamarind dishes, spicy pickles and chutneys. Coastal cooking uses more fish and coconut, while Rayalaseema has a drier-climate food tradition. Recipes vary across districts and households.

dishes.name: Gongura Pachadi
dishes.descriptor: A sour chutney made from gongura leaves
dishes.overview: Gongura pachadi is made from sour sorrel leaves cooked with chillies and garlic, then ground into a coarse chutney. It is commonly eaten with rice and ghee and is especially associated with the Guntur region.
steps: Wash the leaves and dry them well.
Cook the leaves in a little oil until soft.
Fry the chillies and garlic; add optional spices.
Grind or pound everything with salt into a coarse chutney.
Serve with rice and ghee.
dishes.history: The dish's exact origin is not dated. Gongura is widely used in parts of southern India, but it has a strong place in Andhra cooking, particularly around Guntur. Its sour leaves are used in chutneys and pickles; claims of a specific inventor or date are not established by the cited source.

dishes.name: Pootharekulu
dishes.descriptor: A paper-thin rice sweet from Atreyapuram
dishes.overview: Pootharekulu is made by wrapping sugar or jaggery, ghee and sometimes nuts in very thin rice sheets. It is closely associated with Atreyapuram in the Godavari delta and is also known as Andhra's paper sweet.
steps: Soak and grind rice to make a smooth batter.
Spread a very thin layer over a heated surface and lift the dried sheet carefully.
Add sugar or jaggery and ghee, with optional nuts.
Fold the sheet into a small parcel and allow it to cool.
dishes.history: Pootharekulu has been made in Atreyapuram for generations; reports describe a tradition of about 300 years. Its exact inventor is unknown. The story of a rice sheet forming accidentally on a hot pot is a local account, not proven history. Atreyapuram Pootharekulu received a Geographical Indication registration in 2023.

arunachal-pradesh.name: Arunachal Pradesh
arunachal-pradesh.tagline: Himalayan food traditions built around rice, fermentation and forest produce.
arunachal-pradesh.geography: Arunachal Pradesh lies in the Eastern Himalayas. Its forested hills, deep valleys, heavy rainfall and changing elevations create varied food environments. Rice, maize, millet, bamboo shoots, leafy greens and river fish are important local foods.
arunachal-pradesh.culinaryLandscape: Food varies among the state's Indigenous communities. Fermentation, smoking, boiling and steaming are common techniques. Rice-based foods, bamboo shoots, smoked meat and local greens are important, but ingredients and methods differ between communities.

dishes.name: Apong
dishes.descriptor: A traditional fermented rice drink
dishes.overview: Apong is a fermented rice beverage prepared by several communities in Arunachal Pradesh and neighbouring parts of Northeast India. Rice is mixed with a locally prepared starter culture. Methods and strength vary by community and occasion.
ingredients: Local plant ingredients used in some starter cultures
steps: Cook the rice and let it cool.
Mix in the prepared starter culture.
Keep the mixture in a clean container to ferment.
After fermentation, strain or press the mixture to collect the drink.
dishes.history: The drink's exact age is not established. Research documents rice-based fermented beverages and community-made starter cultures across Northeast India. Apong is part of Indigenous food and social traditions; claims of a specific ancient date should be treated cautiously.

dishes.name: Bamboo Shoot Curry
dishes.descriptor: A regional preparation using tender bamboo shoots
dishes.overview: Bamboo shoot curry is a broad group of preparations found in Arunachal Pradesh. Tender shoots may be cooked with meat or vegetables, chillies and local herbs. Some communities preserve shoots by fermenting or drying them.
ingredients: Pork or other meat (in some versions)
Fermented ingredients or leafy greens (in some versions)
steps: Clean and slice the tender bamboo shoots.
Boil or ferment them according to local practice.
Cook with chillies, ginger, salt and vegetables or meat, if used.
Simmer until tender and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Bamboo shoots are an important seasonal food in Arunachal Pradesh. They are eaten fresh or preserved by fermentation and drying. This is a family of community recipes, not one fixed dish, so a single place or date of origin cannot be assigned.

bihar.name: Bihar
bihar.tagline: A Gangetic food culture shaped by rice, wheat, pulses and sattu.
bihar.geography: Bihar lies mainly in the fertile Gangetic plain, crossed by the Ganga and its tributaries. Rice, wheat, pulses, oilseeds and seasonal vegetables shape everyday cooking. Food traditions vary across the Bhojpuri, Maithil and Magahi regions.
bihar.culinaryLandscape: Sattu, litti, chokha, rice, lentils and regional sweets are prominent in Bihari food culture. Mustard oil, roasted gram flour and seasonal produce appear in many household preparations.

dishes.name: Litti Chokha
dishes.descriptor: Roasted wheat balls with mashed vegetables
dishes.overview: Litti are wheat balls filled with roasted gram flour (sattu), spices and mustard oil. They are roasted over heat and served with chokha, a mash of roasted brinjal, potato or tomato seasoned with garlic, chillies and mustard oil.
steps: Knead wheat flour with water into a firm dough.
Mix sattu with mustard oil, garlic, chillies and salt.
Fill dough portions with the sattu mixture and shape into balls.
Roast until cooked through and browned.
Roast the vegetables, mash with seasoning and serve as chokha.
dishes.history: Litti is strongly associated with Bhojpuri foodways in Bihar and nearby regions. Its exact origin is not documented. Its firm wheat shell and sattu filling make it suitable for roasting and carrying, but popular links to specific ancient events or the 1857 uprising should not be treated as established fact.

dishes.name: Silao Khaja
dishes.descriptor: A crisp, layered sweet from Nalanda
dishes.overview: Silao khaja is a crisp sweet made from thin layers of wheat dough, fried in ghee and coated in sugar syrup. It is closely associated with Silao in Nalanda district and is known for its delicate, flaky texture.
steps: Make a firm dough with flour, ghee and water.
Roll it into thin sheets and layer or fold them.
Cut into pieces and deep-fry until crisp.
Coat or soak the pieces in sugar syrup and allow to cool.
dishes.history: Silao is known for its khaja-making tradition and the sweet received a Geographical Indication tag in 2018. Government descriptions note its many thin layers. Stories linking it to the Buddha are presented as local belief, not proven history; the exact origin remains uncertain.

chhattisgarh.name: Chhattisgarh
chhattisgarh.tagline: A rice and forest food culture shaped by seasonal produce and Bastar traditions.
chhattisgarh.geography: Chhattisgarh includes the central plains and the forested Bastar region. Rice is a major crop in the plains, while forests provide bamboo shoots, mushrooms, tubers and leafy greens. The Mahanadi and its tributaries support farming and settlement.
chhattisgarh.culinaryLandscape: Rice, lentils, seasonal vegetables and forest produce are central to many Chhattisgarhi meals. Bastar food traditions include bamboo shoots and locally gathered ingredients. Practices differ between the plains and forest communities.

dishes.name: Chila
dishes.descriptor: A savoury rice-and-lentil pancake
dishes.overview: Chila is a thin pancake made from a batter of soaked rice and urad dal. It is cooked on a griddle and served hot with chutney or curd. It is a familiar breakfast or light meal in Chhattisgarh.
steps: Soak the rice and urad dal for several hours.
Grind with water into a smooth batter.
Add salt and optional herbs or chilli.
Spread on a hot, lightly oiled griddle and cook both sides.
Serve with chutney or curd.
dishes.history: Chila is listed among Chhattisgarh's local foods. Its exact origin is not recorded, and similar rice-and-lentil pancakes are found elsewhere in India. In Chhattisgarh, it reflects the importance of rice and lentils in everyday cooking.

dishes.descriptor: A Bastar vegetable curry traditionally cooked with bamboo
dishes.overview: Aamat is a sour, spiced vegetable preparation from Bastar. It uses mixed vegetables with ginger, garlic and spices; traditional versions include bamboo shoots and may be cooked in bamboo, which adds aroma.
steps: Clean and chop the vegetables and bamboo shoots.
Prepare a base with ginger, garlic and spices.
Combine with the vegetables and a little water.
Cook slowly until tender; traditional versions may use bamboo as a cooking vessel.
Serve with rice.

goa.name: Goa
goa.tagline: A Konkan coastal cuisine shaped by seafood, coconut and Portuguese-era exchange.
goa.geography: Goa lies on the Arabian Sea, with a coastline, laterite plateaus, rivers and the Western Ghats. Its tropical climate supports rice, coconut, cashew, spices, fish and fruit. The coast and rivers have connected Goa to maritime trade for centuries.
goa.culinaryLandscape: Goan food includes distinct Hindu and Catholic traditions. Rice, fish, coconut, kokum, vinegar and spices are widely used; Portuguese rule also influenced some local ingredients, baked foods and cooking practices.

dishes.name: Xacuti
dishes.descriptor: A Goan curry made with roasted spices and coconut
dishes.overview: Xacuti is a rich curry made with roasted spices, coconut and onion. It may be prepared with chicken, meat, seafood or vegetables. It is commonly served with rice or local breads.
steps: Roast coconut, chillies and whole spices until fragrant.
Grind with garlic, ginger and turmeric into a paste.
Cook the onion until soft, then add the main ingredient.
Add the paste and water; simmer until cooked and thickened.
Serve with rice or Goan bread.
dishes.history: Xacuti is part of Goa's wider Konkani food tradition. Its exact origin as a named dish is not documented. Goan cuisine reflects coastal trade and long contact between local communities and Portuguese rule, but the available sources do not establish a single inventor or date for xacuti.

dishes.name: Bebinca
dishes.descriptor: A layered Goan sweet made with coconut milk and egg yolks
dishes.overview: Bebinca is a rich layered dessert made from egg yolks, coconut milk, sugar, flour and ghee. Each thin layer is baked before the next is added. It is especially associated with Goan Catholic celebrations and Christmas.
steps: Mix egg yolks, coconut milk, sugar and flour into a smooth batter.
Grease a baking dish with ghee and pour in a thin layer.
Bake until set, then add another layer.
Repeat until the desired layers are formed.
Cool before slicing.
dishes.history: Bebinca reflects Goa's layered culinary history, combining local coconut with baking traditions shaped during Portuguese rule. A popular story credits Sister Bebiana of the Convent of Santa Monica in Old Goa with creating it. This remains a story rather than a conclusively documented origin.

haryana.name: Haryana
haryana.tagline: A wheat-and-millet cuisine shaped by dry plains and dairy farming.
haryana.geography: Haryana lies on the semi-arid plains west of Delhi. Wheat, bajra, gram, mustard and dairy are important to its farming economy.
haryana.culinaryLandscape: Haryanvi meals often feature bajra roti, khichdi, kadhi, ghee, butter and buttermilk. Recipes vary between drier western districts and the more irrigated Yamuna belt.

dishes.name: Bajra Khichdi
dishes.descriptor: A warming pearl-millet and lentil preparation
dishes.overview: Bajra khichdi combines pearl millet and moong dal into a soft, hearty winter meal. It is served with ghee, butter, jaggery or buttermilk and is associated with Makar Sankranti in parts of Haryana.
steps: Wash the millet and dal.
Cook with water and salt until soft and thick.
Finish with ghee and serve with butter, jaggery or buttermilk.
dishes.history: The dish reflects Haryana’s dryland farming, where bajra is a dependable crop. It is associated with winter and Makar Sankranti, but its exact origin is not documented; it is best seen as a local form of millet khichdi.

dishes.name: Haryanvi Kadhi
dishes.descriptor: A yogurt-and-gram-flour curry
dishes.overview: Haryanvi kadhi is a tangy yogurt-and-gram-flour curry, sometimes served with besan pakoras. It is commonly paired with bajra roti, rice or khichdi.
steps: Whisk yogurt, besan and water until smooth.
Prepare a tempering with ghee or oil, seeds, chillies and turmeric.
Add the yogurt mixture and simmer gently, stirring.
Add pakoras if desired; cook until thick and serve.

himachal-pradesh.name: Himachal Pradesh
himachal-pradesh.tagline: A Himalayan food culture of ceremonial feasts and steamed breads.
himachal-pradesh.geography: Himachal Pradesh spans the western Himalayas, from lower valleys to high mountain settlements. Terraced fields, orchards, barley, millets, lentils and livestock shape local food.
himachal-pradesh.culinaryLandscape: Rice, wheat, lentils, dairy and mountain herbs are widely used. Temple festivals and community gatherings sustain regional feast traditions, while recipes differ between valleys and elevations.

dishes.name: Himachali Dham
dishes.descriptor: A ceremonial vegetarian feast served on leaf plates
dishes.overview: Dham is a ceremonial vegetarian feast served at weddings, festivals and religious gatherings. It can include rice, madra, lentils and sweetened rice, traditionally served on leaf plates and prepared by cooks known as botis.

Cook madra by simmering beans in a spiced yogurt gravy.
Prepare a sweet rice dish where included.
Serve the courses in order on leaf plates at a community gathering.

dishes.overview: Siddu is a fermented, steamed wheat bread from Himachal’s hill regions. It may contain poppy seeds, walnuts or lentils and is served with ghee, dal or meat curry.

jharkhand.name: Jharkhand
jharkhand.tagline: A forest-and-field cuisine shaped by rice and seasonal gathering.
jharkhand.geography: Jharkhand lies on the forested Chota Nagpur Plateau. Rice farming and monsoon cycles shape food, while forests provide mushrooms, tubers, greens and other seasonal produce.
jharkhand.culinaryLandscape: Food traditions vary among Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Ho and other communities. Rice, lentils, mustard oil, fermented foods and gathered forest ingredients are important.

dishes.name: Dhuska
dishes.descriptor: A deep-fried rice-and-lentil pancake
dishes.overview: Dhuska is a crisp, deep-fried snack made from soaked rice and lentils. It is commonly served with potato curry, gram curry or chutney and is popular in Jharkhand.
steps: Soak rice and lentils, then grind with water into a thick batter.
Mix in salt and optional aromatics.
Fry small portions until golden and crisp.
Serve hot with curry or chutney.

Heat mustard oil and cook the spices and optional aromatics.
Add mushrooms and a little water.

madhya-pradesh.name: Madhya Pradesh
madhya-pradesh.tagline: A central Indian cuisine of wheat, lentils and Malwa street food.
madhya-pradesh.geography: Madhya Pradesh includes the Malwa plateau, Vindhya and Satpura ranges, and the Narmada and Chambal river valleys. Wheat, soybean, pulses, millets and forest produce shape its food regions.
madhya-pradesh.culinaryLandscape: Cuisine differs across Malwa, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand and tribal regions. Poha, dal bafla, wheat breads, lentils, gram flour and dairy are prominent, alongside local grain and forest foods.

dishes.name: Indori Poha
dishes.descriptor: A flattened-rice breakfast associated with Indore
dishes.overview: Indori poha is flattened rice cooked with onion, potato, peanuts, spices and lemon. It is a signature Indore breakfast, often served with sev and jalebi.
steps: Rinse and drain the flattened rice.
Temper mustard seeds and curry leaves; cook onion and potato until soft.
Add turmeric, salt and poha; toss until heated through.
Finish with lemon and peanuts; serve with sev or jalebi.

Shape into balls and boil until partly cooked.
Roast or bake until the outside is crisp.
Cook the dal with spices and serve with bafla, ghee and chutney.
dishes.history: Dal bafla is a Malwa variation related to Rajasthan’s dal baati. Its exact origin is not documented. The dish reflects shared regional food traditions, wheat cultivation and the use of ghee in Malwa.

manipur.culinaryLandscape: Meitei food often features rice, fermented fish, vegetables, herbs and chillies. Naga, Kuki, Pangal and other communities maintain their own cuisines and ingredients; fermentation is an important preservation technique.

dishes.name: Eromba
dishes.descriptor: A Meitei mashed vegetable and fermented-fish dish
dishes.overview: Eromba, or iromba, is a Meitei dish of boiled vegetables mashed with chillies and fermented fish called ngari. It is usually eaten with rice and has a strong, savoury flavour.
steps: Boil or steam the vegetables until soft.
Roast or soften the chillies.
Mash the vegetables with chillies and salt.
Mix in ngari and serve with rice.

meghalaya.geography: Meghalaya's rainy plateau, hills and valleys support rice, maize, millet, citrus and livestock. Forests and rivers also provide seasonal greens, fish and bamboo shoots.
meghalaya.culinaryLandscape: Khasi, Jaintia and Garo cuisines use rice, smoked meat, fermented soybeans, bamboo shoots and wild greens. Fermentation, smoking and drying help preserve food.

dishes.name: Jadoh
dishes.descriptor: Khasi rice cooked with meat and spices
dishes.overview: Jadoh is rice cooked with pork or chicken, turmeric, ginger and aromatic leaves. It is eaten in Khasi homes and at community gatherings, often with chutney or pickle.
steps: Cook the meat with ginger, onion, turmeric and bay leaf.
Add washed rice and enough water.
Simmer until the rice is tender and absorbs the meat's flavour.
Serve hot with chutney or pickle.
dishes.history: Jadoh is closely associated with Khasi food culture, where rice and meat feature in everyday and communal meals. Its precise origin is not documented; it reflects local ingredients and a simple one-pot cooking style.

Pack them in a leaf-lined basket and ferment for several days.
Cook the fermented beans with onion, ginger, garlic and chillies.

mizoram.name: Mizoram

mizoram.geography: Mizoram's steep, rainy hills and forests support shifting cultivation, bamboo, rice, ginger, chillies and leafy greens. Pork and freshwater fish are also important foods.
mizoram.culinaryLandscape: Mizo cooking often uses boiling, steaming, smoking and fermentation, with relatively little oil. Rice, vegetables, bamboo shoots, pork and preserved ingredients are common.

dishes.name: Bai
dishes.descriptor: A Mizo stew of seasonal vegetables and greens
dishes.overview: Bai is a flexible stew of vegetables, leafy greens and sometimes edible ferns. Some versions use fermented pork fat or bamboo shoots; it is usually served with rice.
steps: Wash and chop the vegetables and greens.
Boil them with salt and water until tender.
Add fermented pork fat or optional seasonings.
Simmer briefly and serve with rice.

Smoke the meat over a hearth.
Dry until firm and preserved.
Cook with vegetables or bamboo shoots and serve with rice.

nagaland.geography: Nagaland's forested hills and high rainfall support rice, maize, millet, bamboo and shifting cultivation. Its location near Myanmar has long enabled regional exchange.
nagaland.culinaryLandscape: Naga food traditions vary among communities such as the Ao, Angami, Sema and Lotha. Pork, bamboo shoots, fermented soybean, chillies and smoked foods are widely used, often with little oil.

dishes.name: Smoked Pork with Bamboo Shoot
dishes.descriptor: A smoky Naga pork dish with bamboo shoots
dishes.overview: Pork is smoked over a hearth and cooked with bamboo shoots, chillies and local herbs. The dish is commonly served with rice and reflects Naga traditions of smoking and preserving food.

Clean and slice the bamboo shoots.
Cook the pork with bamboo shoots, chillies and salt.
Simmer until tender and serve with rice.

odisha.geography: Odisha stretches from the Bay of Bengal coast to the Eastern Ghats and forested interior. The Mahanadi delta supports rice farming, while coastal communities also use fish and seafood.
odisha.culinaryLandscape: Odia meals commonly feature rice, lentils, vegetables and mustard oil. Jagannath Temple food traditions, coastal cooking and Indigenous foodways all shape the state's cuisine.

dishes.name: Dalma
dishes.descriptor: An Odia stew of lentils and vegetables
dishes.overview: Dalma combines lentils with vegetables such as pumpkin, raw banana and brinjal, seasoned with ginger and cumin. It is eaten with rice in homes and is also associated with temple food traditions.
steps: Cook the lentils with turmeric and salt.
Add chopped vegetables, ginger and cumin.
Simmer until the lentils and vegetables are soft.
Finish with optional coconut or a ghee tempering; serve with rice.
dishes.history: Dalma is strongly associated with Odia home cooking and Jagannath food traditions. Accounts linking it to the Savara people are cultural traditions rather than firmly established history; its exact origin is unknown.

Mix with sugar, cardamom and optional nuts.
Shape into a cake and bake slowly until the crust caramelises.
Cool, slice and serve.

sikkim.geography: Sikkim's steep elevation range creates climates from subtropical valleys to alpine areas. Rice, maize, millet, cardamom, ginger, dairy and mountain greens are important foods.
sikkim.culinaryLandscape: Sikkimese food reflects Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali communities. Fermentation, steaming and preservation are common, alongside rice, dairy, meat and Himalayan greens.

dishes.descriptor: A Bhutia stew of pork, radish and chillies
dishes.overview: Phagshapa is a pork stew cooked with radish and chillies. It is associated with Bhutia food culture and is commonly served with rice.

Add sliced radish and salt.
Simmer until the pork is tender and the radish is soft.
Serve hot with rice.

Pack them tightly in a clean container and allow them to ferment.
Remove the fermented greens and dry them in the sun.
Rehydrate and cook in soup or curry.

telangana.geography: Telangana occupies the semi-arid Deccan Plateau, crossed by the Godavari and Krishna rivers. Rice, millets, pulses, groundnuts and chillies shape its agriculture.
telangana.culinaryLandscape: Rural Telangana cooking features millets, tamarind, sesame, lentils and flatbreads. Hyderabad adds a distinct courtly tradition shaped by Deccan and Mughal influences.

dishes.name: Hyderabadi Biryani
dishes.descriptor: A layered rice-and-meat dish shaped by Deccan and Mughal traditions
dishes.overview: A layered rice-and-meat dish flavoured with yogurt, saffron and whole spices. It is associated with Hyderabad’s Asaf Jahi court and is served with raita or mirchi ka salan.

Parboil the rice with whole spices.
Layer rice and meat in a heavy pot; add ghee and saffron.
Seal and cook slowly using the dum method.
Serve with raita or mirchi ka salan.
dishes.history: Hyderabadi biryani developed in the courtly food culture of the Asaf Jahi Nizams, drawing on Mughal, Persian and Deccan traditions. Late nineteenth-century Hyderabadi cookbooks document a varied biryani tradition; no single inventor is established.

uttarakhand.culinaryLandscape: Kumaoni and Garhwali cooking relies on grains, lentils, dairy and seasonal forest produce. Simple, warming dishes and preserved foods suit the mountain climate.

Boil or steam until soft, then mash or grind.
Cook with garlic, chillies and salt.
Stir in rice flour and simmer until thick.

andaman-and-nicobar-islands.name: Andaman and Nicobar Islands
andaman-and-nicobar-islands.tagline: Island foodways shaped by seafood, coconut, tubers and migration.
andaman-and-nicobar-islands.geography: This Bay of Bengal archipelago includes two island groups separated by the Ten Degree Channel. Tropical forests, coral waters and a maritime climate support fishing, coconut and tuber cultivation. The Andamans and Nicobars have distinct communities and food histories.
andaman-and-nicobar-islands.culinaryLandscape: Seafood is prominent in the Andamans, where Bengali, South Indian and other migrant food traditions are visible. Nicobarese foodways place particular importance on coconut, tubers, pig and marine foods. These traditions should not be treated as one uniform island cuisine.

dishes.name: Andaman Fish Curry
dishes.descriptor: A coastal fish curry served with rice
dishes.overview: A flexible island-style curry made with locally caught fish, coconut, chilli and souring ingredients. Recipes vary across communities and islands, reflecting the region's seafood economy and the influence of Bengali and South Indian cooking. It is commonly served with rice.

Prepare a curry base with chilli, turmeric, tamarind and aromatics.
Add coconut milk or coconut and enough water to form a light gravy.
Add the fish and simmer gently until cooked.
Adjust seasoning and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Fish curry reflects the islands' marine food economy, but there is no single documented origin or fixed recipe. Official tourism material describes fresh seafood and Bengali-style fish preparations among the foods available in the Andamans. The dish is best presented as a living coastal food tradition shaped by local catch and migration, not as one uniform Indigenous recipe.

chandigarh.name: Chandigarh
chandigarh.tagline: A planned city with Punjabi, Haryanvi and contemporary urban food influences.
chandigarh.geography: Chandigarh sits on the plains at the Shivalik foothills, between Punjab and Haryana. Developed as a planned city in the twentieth century, it grew through migration and urban expansion rather than an ancient, separate regional food system.
chandigarh.culinaryLandscape: Punjabi food is highly visible in Chandigarh, alongside Haryanvi and wider North Indian influences. Wheat breads, dairy, tandoori cooking, chickpeas and street snacks feature prominently. The city's restaurants and markets reflect a modern, mixed urban population.

dishes.name: Chole Bhature
dishes.descriptor: Spiced chickpeas with deep-fried leavened bread
dishes.overview: Chole bhature pairs chickpeas simmered in a spiced gravy with puffy, deep-fried bread. It is a popular breakfast and street-food choice in Chandigarh, reflecting the city's Punjabi food culture rather than a dish invented locally.
steps: Soak and cook the chickpeas until tender.
Prepare a masala with onion, tomato, ginger, garlic and spices.
Simmer the chickpeas in the masala.
Make and rest a soft dough for the bhature.
Roll and deep-fry the breads until puffed; serve hot with chole.
dishes.history: Chole bhature belongs to the wider Punjabi and North Indian food tradition. It became a familiar part of Chandigarh's urban dining scene as the planned city grew and drew residents from nearby regions. Its precise origin is debated, so it should not be presented as a uniquely Chandigarh invention.

dishes.name: Amritsari Kulcha
dishes.descriptor: A stuffed Punjabi flatbread baked in a tandoor
dishes.overview: Amritsari kulcha is a leavened flatbread stuffed with potato, onion or paneer and baked in a tandoor. Served with chole, chutney or butter, it is associated with Amritsar but is widely enjoyed in Chandigarh's Punjabi-influenced food scene.
steps: Prepare a soft dough and let it rest.
Season mashed potato or another chosen filling.
Fill and roll the dough into a flatbread.
Bake in a hot tandoor or cook on a suitable griddle.
Brush with ghee or butter and serve with chole.
dishes.history: Amritsari kulcha is a Punjabi specialty associated with Amritsar, not a Chandigarh-origin dish. Its popularity in Chandigarh reflects the movement of Punjabi food traditions across the region and the city's shared dining culture. The exact age of the named preparation is not firmly established.

dadra-and-nagar-haveli-and-daman-and-diu.name: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
dadra-and-nagar-haveli-and-daman-and-diu.tagline: Inland Adivasi foodways meet the coastal and Portuguese-influenced traditions of Daman and Diu.
dadra-and-nagar-haveli-and-daman-and-diu.geography: The Union Territory combines inland Dadra and Nagar Haveli, near Gujarat and Maharashtra, with the Arabian Sea enclaves of Daman and Diu. Forests, rivers and tribal settlements shape inland foodways, while fishing, coconut and maritime contact influence the coast.
dadra-and-nagar-haveli-and-daman-and-diu.culinaryLandscape: Food traditions differ across the territory. Adivasi communities in Dadra and Nagar Haveli use rice, millets, tubers and forest produce. Daman and Diu draw on Gujarati coastal cooking and Portuguese-era influences, visible in seafood and layered sweets such as bebinca.

dishes.name: Ukad
dishes.descriptor: A steamed rice-flour preparation associated with Dadra and Nagar Haveli
dishes.overview: Ukad is identified in a NITI Aayog regional profile as a traditional tribal preparation made from rice flour and served with spicy chutneys or curries. It reflects the use of rice and simple, locally available accompaniments in the food culture of Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
ingredients: Chilli chutney or curry to serve
steps: Mix rice flour with water and salt to make a thick mixture.
Cook or steam it until the rice flour is fully set.
Shape or portion while warm, according to local practice.
Serve with spicy chutney or curry.
dishes.history: The NITI Aayog profile identifies ukad as a traditional tribal rice-flour food of Dadra and Nagar Haveli. The available reference does not establish a precise date or inventor, so the dish is best presented as a continuing regional food practice rather than assigned a specific origin story.

dishes.name: Bebinca of Diu
dishes.descriptor: A layered coconut-and-egg sweet shaped by Indo-Portuguese foodways
dishes.overview: Bebinca is a rich layered sweet made with coconut milk, eggs, flour, sugar and ghee. In Diu it reflects the territory's Portuguese-era connections and is served as a dessert or festive treat. Thin layers are baked one after another to create its characteristic texture.
steps: Whisk coconut milk, eggs, sugar and flour into a smooth batter.
Grease a baking dish with ghee.
Pour a thin layer and bake until set and lightly coloured.
Repeat with further layers, brushing with ghee as needed.
Cool before slicing and serving.
dishes.history: Diu's food culture reflects centuries of Portuguese presence, which ended in 1961. Incredible India identifies bebinca among the island's culinary offerings and describes its layered coconut-based preparation. The dessert is shared across parts of the former Portuguese coastal world; it should not be described as exclusive to Diu.

delhi.name: Delhi
delhi.tagline: A capital food culture shaped by Mughal courts, street markets and Punjabi migration.
delhi.geography: Delhi lies on the Yamuna plain at a historic crossroads of northern India. Its position as a political and trading centre encouraged migration and exchange over centuries. Wheat, dairy, pulses, spices and market foods remain important to its varied food culture.
delhi.culinaryLandscape: Delhi's cuisine brings together Mughal and North Indian traditions, Old Delhi street food, Punjabi migration after Partition and newer urban influences. Kebabs, breads, biryani, chaat and restaurant dishes such as butter chicken illustrate this layered history.

dishes.name: Butter Chicken
dishes.descriptor: Tandoori chicken in a tomato, butter and cream gravy
dishes.overview: Butter chicken, or murgh makhani, combines tandoor-cooked chicken with a smooth tomato-and-butter sauce. It is closely associated with Moti Mahal in Daryaganj and Delhi's post-Partition restaurant culture. Its creamy gravy and smoky chicken made it a widely copied restaurant dish.
steps: Marinate chicken in yogurt, ginger, garlic and spices.
Roast or grill the chicken until cooked and lightly charred.
Cook tomatoes with butter and spices to make the gravy.
Blend or strain the gravy, then add the chicken.
Simmer briefly and finish with cream if desired.
dishes.history: Butter chicken emerged in the mid-twentieth-century Punjabi restaurant world linked to Moti Mahal in Daryaganj. The exact inventor remains disputed between families connected with the restaurant, and some accounts trace the story to pre-Partition Peshawar. Delhi Tourism places its emergence at Moti Mahal in the 1950s; the competing claims should remain visible rather than be presented as settled fact.

dishes.name: Old Delhi Chaat
dishes.descriptor: Tangy street snacks built around potato, crisp breads and chutneys
dishes.overview: Chaat is a family of street foods combining ingredients such as potato, crisp fried dough, gram, yogurt, chutneys and tangy spices. Chandni Chowk is strongly associated with these snacks, whose varieties differ from vendor to vendor.
steps: Boil and chop the potatoes; cook chickpeas if using.
Arrange papdi or another crisp base on a plate.
Add potato, chickpeas and yogurt.
Top with tamarind and mint chutneys and spice mix.
Serve immediately while the crisp elements remain crunchy.
dishes.history: Chaat is deeply associated with Old Delhi's market streets, especially Chandni Chowk. Delhi Tourism describes combinations of potato, crisp fried bread, dahi bhalla, gram and tangy-salty spices. Its exact origin is uncertain; popular stories connecting it to a particular Mughal ruler are not firmly documented.

jammu-and-kashmir.name: Jammu and Kashmir
jammu-and-kashmir.tagline: A Himalayan food culture with Kashmiri Pandit, Muslim and Wazwan traditions.
jammu-and-kashmir.geography: The Union Territory includes the Kashmir Valley, Jammu plains and Himalayan ranges. The valley supports rice, saffron, walnut and apple cultivation, while the Jammu region has different climates and crops. Mountain routes and historic trade connected the region with Central and South Asia.
jammu-and-kashmir.culinaryLandscape: Kashmiri food traditions include household cooking, Kashmiri Pandit preparations and the elaborate Muslim Wazwan feast. Rice, lamb, yogurt, saffron, dried chillies and aromatic spices are common, but recipes and food practices vary by community and region.

dishes.name: Rogan Josh
dishes.descriptor: A Kashmiri lamb curry served in household meals and Wazwan
dishes.overview: Rogan josh is a slow-cooked lamb curry flavoured with Kashmiri chillies, fennel, ginger and other spices. Recipes differ between Kashmiri Pandit and Muslim traditions, including their use of garlic, yogurt and colouring agents. It is also recognised as a Wazwan dish.
steps: Brown the lamb in heated oil or ghee.
Add whole spices, ginger and ground Kashmiri chilli.
Add water or yogurt according to the chosen regional style.
Simmer slowly until the lamb is tender and the gravy is aromatic.
Serve with rice.
dishes.history: Rogan josh is a recognised part of Kashmiri cuisine and is served in Wazwan, the multi-course feast prepared for weddings and other gatherings. Its history is often linked to Persian and Central Asian influences, but a precise date or single inventor is not established. Regional and community versions should not be collapsed into one standard recipe.

dishes.name: Kashmiri Kahwa
dishes.descriptor: Green tea infused with saffron, nuts and warm spices
dishes.overview: Kahwa is a fragrant green tea brewed with ingredients such as saffron, cardamom, cinnamon and almonds. It is served at gatherings, celebrations and as a gesture of hospitality. Recipes vary between households and may include honey or sugar.
steps: Simmer water with cardamom and cinnamon.
Add green tea and steep briefly.
Place saffron and sliced almonds in serving cups.
Strain the tea into the cups and sweeten if desired.
Serve hot.
dishes.history: Kahwa is associated with Kashmiri hospitality and is served at weddings, festivals and religious gatherings. Its use of green tea, saffron, nuts and spices reflects the region's agricultural and trading connections. The exact date of its arrival in Kashmir is uncertain, so claims of a precise origin should be avoided.

ladakh.name: Ladakh
ladakh.tagline: A high-altitude food culture shaped by barley, root vegetables and Tibetan exchange.
ladakh.geography: Ladakh is a high-altitude trans-Himalayan region with cold deserts, short growing seasons and the Indus valley. Barley, buckwheat, peas, apricots and livestock are important to local food systems. Historic routes connected Ladakh with Tibet and Central Asia.
ladakh.culinaryLandscape: Ladakhi food is adapted to cold and altitude. Barley, wheat, root vegetables, dairy and dried foods feature in everyday meals. Tibetan and Central Asian exchange is visible, but local dishes such as skyu and the salted butter tea gur gur cha have a distinct place in Ladakhi food culture.

dishes.name: Skyu
dishes.descriptor: A Ladakhi stew of small dough pieces and root vegetables
dishes.overview: Skyu is a hearty Ladakhi stew made with small pieces of wheat dough simmered with root vegetables. Meat may be added, while vegetarian versions are also prepared. Its thick, warming consistency suits the cold climate and makes it a distinctive local comfort food.
steps: Knead flour, water and salt into a firm dough.
Pinch or roll the dough into small pieces.
Cook onion and root vegetables in a pot with water or stock.
Add the dough pieces and simmer until tender.
Add meat or seasoning if used, and serve hot.
dishes.history: Skyu is identified in educational documentation on Leh-Ladakh as a specifically Ladakhi dish. Its dough-based preparation and use of root vegetables reflect local grain and garden produce, while its dense, warming form suits the high-altitude climate. A precise date or inventor is not documented.

dishes.name: Gur Gur Cha (Butter Tea)
dishes.descriptor: A salted tea churned with butter for warmth and energy
dishes.overview: Gur gur cha is a traditional Ladakhi tea made by combining strong tea with salt and butter, often from yak or other local dairy. It is served hot throughout the day and is closely tied to hospitality and the region's pastoral economy.
steps: Boil tea leaves in water to make a strong infusion.
Add salt and milk if used.
Combine the hot tea with butter in a churn.
Churn until the drink is blended and lightly frothy.
Serve hot.
dishes.history: Salted butter tea is a long-standing drink across Tibetan Himalayan communities and is central to Ladakhi hospitality. It uses local dairy and provides a warming, energy-rich drink in a cold, high-altitude environment. It is shared across the wider Himalayan region, so it should not be described as exclusive to Ladakh.

lakshadweep.name: Lakshadweep
lakshadweep.tagline: An island food culture centred on tuna, coconut, rice and Minicoy traditions.
lakshadweep.geography: Lakshadweep is an archipelago of coral atolls in the Arabian Sea. Its small land area limits cultivation, while surrounding waters support tuna and reef fishing. Proximity to Kerala and the Maldives has shaped language, trade and food traditions across the islands.
lakshadweep.culinaryLandscape: Tuna, coconut and rice are central to Lakshadweep's food system. Minicoy has distinctive cultural links with the Maldives, visible in dishes such as mus kavaab. Drying and processing tuna, including the production of masmin, are important to island livelihoods and cuisine.

dishes.name: Mus Kavaab
dishes.descriptor: A spiced tuna preparation associated with Minicoy
dishes.overview: Mus kavaab is a Minicoy speciality made with tuna, chilli, coriander and cardamom, cooked with onion, curry leaves and tomato. It reflects the island's seafood-based cuisine and its cultural links with the Maldives. It is distinct from the coconut-and-jaggery sweets also found across the islands.
steps: Clean and cut the tuna into pieces.
Season with chilli, coriander, cardamom and salt.
Cook onion, tomato and curry leaves in a pan.
Add the tuna and cook until done, allowing the spices to coat it.
Serve with rice or flatbread.
dishes.history: Incredible India identifies mus kavaab as a Minicoy speciality and describes its tuna-and-spice preparation. The dish reflects the island's strong tuna fishery and cultural connections across the Maldives region. Its exact date of origin is not documented.

dishes.name: Maas Podichathu
dishes.descriptor: Dried tuna mixed with coconut and spices
dishes.overview: Maas podichathu combines dried tuna with coconut, turmeric, onion and garlic. It draws on Lakshadweep's tuna fishery and the preservation of fish for later use. The preparation is a flavourful accompaniment to rice and other island dishes.
steps: Prepare or obtain dried tuna and break it into small flakes.
Grate the coconut and finely chop the aromatics.
Combine tuna with coconut, turmeric, onion, garlic and chilli.
Mix or lightly cook until the flavours combine.
Serve as an accompaniment with rice.
dishes.history: Maas podichathu is listed by Incredible India among Lakshadweep's traditional foods and uses dried tuna with coconut and aromatics. puducherry.name: Puducherry
puducherry.tagline: A Tamil coastal food culture with French and Creole influences in selected dishes.
puducherry.geography: The Union Territory includes Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam, separated geographically and shaped by neighbouring regions. The Coromandel coast, rivers and fishing settlements support rice, seafood, coconut and tamarind. French rule left a visible but uneven influence on local foodways.
puducherry.culinaryLandscape: Puducherry's food is fundamentally diverse and largely Tamil, with distinct community traditions and influences from Telugu, Malayalam and French-speaking households. Everyday foods such as sambar coexist with bakery breads and selected Franco-Tamil or Creole preparations. The four enclaves should not be treated as culturally identical.

dishes.name: Roll Roti
dishes.descriptor: A local bakery bread linked to Franco-Tamil household foodways
dishes.overview: Roll roti is a bread associated with older wood-fired bakeries in Puducherry. Tamil cooks supplied bread to French and Creole households, and it was eaten with sweetened tea or coconut milk. The preparation is a record of everyday exchange rather than simply a French dish transplanted to India.
ingredients: Coconut milk or tea to serve
steps: Mix flour, water, salt and leavening into a dough.
Knead and rest until the dough becomes workable.
Shape into small rolls or flat rounds.
Bake in a hot oven until cooked and lightly browned.
Serve with tea or coconut milk, as preferred.
dishes.history: Sahapedia documents roll roti as a bread made by Tamil bakers for households in colonial Puducherry. Wood-fired bakeries supplied French and Creole homes, and the bread was also eaten by local workers. The story complicates the idea that Puducherry cuisine is simply French: local cooks and Tamil tastes shaped these exchanges.

dishes.name: Vettu Sambar
dishes.descriptor: A simple Tamil home-style sambar from Puducherry foodways
dishes.overview: Vettu sambar is a quick, economical home-style preparation described in accounts of Puducherry's Tamil food culture. It is flavoured with chilli and common pantry ingredients and served with hot rice. Family methods vary, reflecting its place in everyday cooking rather than restaurant cuisine.
steps: Cook the toor dal until soft.
Prepare tamarind water and add chilli and turmeric.
Simmer the tamarind mixture with onion and optional tomato.
Add the cooked dal and simmer until combined.
Temper with mustard seeds and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Sahapedia records vettu sambar through a household account and places it within the everyday Tamil foodways of Puducherry. The dish is valued for its simplicity and affordability. This is a documented living food practice, not a recipe with a known inventor or precise date of origin.
